newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Direct sailings between Taiwan, China foreseen.
newsitem.headline: Direct sailings between Taiwan, China foreseen.

text.p: A leading Taiwan shipper said on Thursday that China appeared to be preparing to allow direct sailings across the Taiwan strait in April -- the first such crossings since 1949.
In response, Taipei cautiously reiterated its conditions for direct links, seeking to ensure the breakthrough did not undermine the sovereignty of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China.
Taiwan media on Thursday said Taiwan shipping leaders had begun receiving invitations for an April 8 ceremony in China's southeastern port of Xiamen to mark the first direct sailing.
Xiamen officials declined to confirm the reports.

At Yangming Marine Transport Corp, spokesman M.S. Tsay declined to say whether Yangming, one of the world's top shipping firms, received an invitation but voiced confidence Beijing would approve its bid to start Taiwan-China routes.
"We are confident that Yangming will be among those getting permission for cross-strait shipping," Tsay told Reuters.
Tsay said Beijing's 54-day review of applications submitted by Yangming and a dozen other Taiwan shippers was under way and that the first approvals were expected in early April.
Industry experts said Taiwan shippers could start operating direct sailings immediately after China granted permission.
Taiwan officials were cautious, saying they had no evidence of China's plans and reiterating Taiwan's basic conditions.

One official in the transport and communications ministry said Taiwan's ports were ready to receive ships sailing directly from China as long as they were owned by mainland, Taiwan or Hong Kong interests and flew a Hong Kong or third-country flag.
"If they meet these two principles and mainland authorities approve, they will be allowed into port," the official told Reuters on condition his name not be used.
The official stressed that under current rules cargoes arriving directly from China could enter Taiwan's Kaohsiung port but would not be allowed to pass through Taiwan customs.

Taiwan has banned direct links since 1949, when the island was separated from the newly communist mainland by a civil war, though indirect cross-strait trade and investment have flourished since a political thaw began in the late 1980s.

Facing intense pressure to ease the ban, Taipei has proposed creating an "offshore transshipment centre" at Kaohsiung, where incoming mainland cargoes could be processed in bonded zones outside Taiwan customs for onward international shipment.

Taking a different tack, Beijing maintains that since Taiwan is part of China, cross-strait shipping is a domestic issue that initially should involve mainland, Taiwan or Hong Kong ships or foreign-flagged ships that are wholly or partially owned by mainland, Taiwan or Hong Kong interests.
Beijing has made no public response to Taiwan's proposal, which strives to preserve the Republic of China's sovereignty by not giving berth to ships flying communist China's flag.
Likewise, Beijing would not welcome any ship flying Taiwan's republican flag as this would contravene Beijing's "one China" principle.
On February 23, the Hong Kong container ship Lien Fung made what experts called the first quasi-direct crossing, passing through Hong Kong harbour en route to Kaohsiung from Xiamen.

That unprecedented passage and several since, widely seen as an incremental easing of Taiwan's ban, was possible under a pact reached in Hong Kong on January 22 by Taiwan and China shipping executives with tacit approval of both governments.
Transshipping across the Taiwan strait has soared in recent years, with Hong Kong cashing in as a middleman.
Experts estimate that cargoes shipped directly between China and Taiwan would cost 40 percent less than indirect shipments.
Yangming estimates direct links would save it U$26.18 million a year.
